claims.text: Mechanically mixed Mg and Co/Cr/Fe/Ni powders are prone to elemental segregation and unstable microstructures during standard sintering.
Elemental segregation and unstable microstructures cause poor oxidation and corrosion resistance in Mg-transition-metal alloys.
Thermolysis of transition-metal dithiocarbamates or analogous molecular precursors can produce multicomponent metal sulfide or oxide materials.
Combining transition-metal dithiocarbamates with Mg salts and thermolyzing them will produce a pre-reacted, atomically mixed Mg-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni powder.
Atomic-scale precursor mixing will suppress elemental segregation in the Mg-transition-metal alloy.
Precursor-derived atomic mixing eliminates the need for high-temperature solid-state diffusion to overcome segregation barriers.
Atomic-scale premixing allows the alloy to bypass a high-energy barrier for nucleation of secondary phases.
The precursor route facilitates a disorder-to-order transition or solid-solution formation in the Mg-transition-metal alloy at 850 °C.
Standard powder mixing requires temperatures above 900 °C for sufficient diffusion in this Mg-transition-metal system.
Applying pressure through SPS or a similar rapid-sintering process enhances densification.
Sintering the precursor-derived alloy at 850 °C will produce greater than 95% theoretical density.
Sintering the precursor-derived alloy at 850 °C will produce a single-phase-like microstructure with a uniform elemental distribution.
Cr-containing CoCrFeNi-based alloys can form Cr2O3 during oxidation.
A continuous MgO/Cr2O3 barrier formed by the proposed alloy will significantly improve oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Segregation produces brittle, spalling oxide layers in the proposed Mg-transition-metal alloy.
Relative density falls below 90% when the sintering temperature is below 800 °C.
Mg loss exceeds 5% when the sintering temperature exceeds 950 °C.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism treat temperatures above 900 °C as the onset of problematic Mg volatility, whereas the quantitative boundary says volatility dominates only above 950 °C.
The prescribed processing conditions say sintering is strictly limited to 800–900 °C, but the falsification experiment includes sintering at 950 °C.
